questions.prompt: A workload needs SQL Server Agent jobs and cross-database queries within the same instance, but the team wants Microsoft to keep patching the OS and the SQL Server engine automatically. Which deployment option fits, and why?
options: Azure SQL Managed Instance — it exposes near-100% of SQL Server's instance-level surface, including Agent jobs and cross-database queries, while Microsoft still patches the OS and the engine
Azure SQL Database — it's the fastest option to provision and is fully patched by Microsoft, so it's the right default regardless of which instance-level features a workload needs
SQL Server on an Azure VM — it provides Agent jobs and cross-database queries natively, and being hosted in Azure means Microsoft automatically patches the OS and SQL Server for you
Either Azure SQL Database or SQL Server on an Azure VM work equally well here, since both sit under the same 'Azure SQL' umbrella term
questions.explain: Azure SQL Database is database-scoped and has no instance-level surface at all — no Agent jobs, no cross-database queries by default. SQL Server on an Azure VM has that surface, but you patch the OS and SQL Server yourself, the same as on-prem. Only Managed Instance gives near-100% of SQL Server's instance-level surface while still being PaaS, with Microsoft handling OS and engine patching.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: "Azure SQL" is not one product you deploy — it's an ________ term Microsoft uses for a family of ways to run SQL Server-compatible workloads in Azure.
questions.explain: Lesson 2 is explicit that Azure SQL is an umbrella term covering three genuinely different products — Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and SQL Server on an Azure VM — each moving a different slice of ownership onto Microsoft, not three pricing tiers of one thing.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 5/6 term to what it actually is.
right: The deepest SQL Server-specific tooling: execution plans, Extended Events, Windows-only
Azure SQL Database's authentication/firewall container — not a physical machine
Provisioning, configuring, scaling, and monitoring Azure resources — not the daily query-writing tool
Cross-platform, notebook-capable, Azure-first query and administration tool
questions.explain: The Azure Portal is the resource's control panel — provisioning, scaling, cost, alerts — not a daily query workbench. SSMS remains the deepest SQL Server-specific tool (execution plans, Extended Events) but is Windows-only. Azure Data Studio is cross-platform and notebook-capable, built Azure-first. A logical server is Azure SQL Database's authentication and firewall container, created before any database can exist inside it — not a physical machine you can see.

questions.code:
SELECT
    DB_NAME()               AS current_database,
    @@SERVERNAME             AS server_name,
    SERVERPROPERTY('Edition') AS edition;
questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 6's lab — building your first Azure SQL environment — in the correct order.
items: Create the logical server and database through the Azure Portal, using SQL authentication and the smallest available compute/storage tier
Open the logical server's Networking blade and add your client IPv4 address as a firewall rule
Connect to the database from SSMS using the logical server's full .database.windows.net name and the SQL login created in Step 1
Run the SELECT query above and confirm the returned edition string contains "SQL Azure"
questions.explain: The lab's chain only works in this order: the logical server and database have to exist first, then the firewall rule has to be added before any connection is allowed at all — a freshly created server rejects every connection by default, including your own — and only then can SSMS actually connect, at which point the SELECT query proves the Portal deployment, the firewall rule, and SSMS connectivity all genuinely work together.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the DTU and vCore purchasing models, per Chapter 2.
options: A DTU bundles compute, memory, and I/O into a single number, with one tier and count to size the whole database
The vCore model prices and sizes compute and storage independently of each other
Azure Hybrid Benefit can be applied to a DTU-based database as long as the organization already owns a SQL Server license
Business Critical and Hyperscale service tiers exist only under the vCore model — there's no DTU equivalent
Serverless compute is available on the Business Critical and Hyperscale tiers in most regions, the same as on General Purpose
questions.explain: A DTU really is one blended number covering compute, memory, and I/O. vCore genuinely separates compute pricing from storage pricing — which is exactly why Azure Hybrid Benefit requires the vCore model: it discounts the compute line item specifically, and DTU pricing never separated one out. Business Critical and Hyperscale exist only under vCore. Serverless is only available on General Purpose in most regions, not Business Critical or Hyperscale, which are provisioned-only.

questions.prompt: A SaaS vendor runs 200 tenant databases, each with unpredictable usage spikes that rarely all happen at the same time. Which compute approach fits best, and why?
options: An elastic pool — a shared compute/storage budget that all 200 member databases draw from as needed, instead of every tenant being sized for its own worst case
Serverless compute configured individually on each of the 200 databases, since serverless auto-pauses whichever database is currently idle
Provisioned compute, with every one of the 200 databases sized at its own individual peak usage
Azure SQL Managed Instance, since only an instance can host multiple tenant databases under one deployment
questions.explain: An elastic pool solves exactly this shape of problem: many databases that each spike at different, unpredictable times share one eDTU/vCore budget instead of each being provisioned for its own worst case, which would be expensive capacity sitting unused most of the time. Serverless solves one database's own idle-vs-spiky pattern, not sharing capacity across many databases. Managed Instance can host many databases too, but that's not what actually solves the uncorrelated-spike cost problem — the elastic pool mechanism does.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Azure SQL Managed Instance requires a dedicated subnet inside a ________, delegated specifically to Managed Instance and used by nothing else — a precondition for creation, not optional configuration added later.
questions.explain: Managed Instance's near-100% SQL Server surface depends on network isolation a shared multi-tenant database can't offer, so a delegated subnet inside a Virtual Network has to exist before creation even starts — unlike Azure SQL Database's firewall rule, which can be added at any time after the database already exists.

questions.prompt: Match each service tier to what it's actually for, per Lessons 8-11.
right: Balanced compute/storage/price; most production vCore workloads, remote storage
Highest resilience and lowest latency; local SSD, built-in read replica
Most general-purpose production workloads under the DTU model
Very large (multi-TB+) databases needing fast scaling and backups
questions.explain: Standard is the DTU model's general-purpose production tier. Business Critical trades higher cost per GB for local SSD storage and a built-in read replica, which is also why it supports read scale-out. Hyperscale's distributed storage architecture is built for multi-TB+ databases that need fast scaling and backups. General Purpose is the vCore model's balanced, remote-storage default.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about table partitioning, per Lesson 15.
options: Table partitioning is unrelated to the OVER (PARTITION BY ...) clause used in window functions, despite sharing a word
A partition FUNCTION defines the boundary values that split a column's range into pieces, and a partition SCHEME maps each of those pieces onto a filegroup
The primary reason to partition a large table is faster queries; faster maintenance is only a secondary bonus
ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD PARTITION = 3 can rebuild one partition's index without touching the rest of a multi-hundred-million-row table
Partition elimination lets the optimizer skip partitions based on a filter on any column in the table, not specifically the partitioning column
questions.explain: Table partitioning is a physical storage decision, genuinely unrelated to the window-function PARTITION BY clause. The partition function sets the boundary values; the partition scheme maps those ranges onto filegroups. Rebuilding one named partition instead of the whole table is exactly the maintenance win Lesson 15 calls payoff #1 — and that maintenance win, not faster queries, is the primary driver; partition elimination is described as a bonus, not the main reason, and it only triggers when the filter is on the partitioning column itself.

questions.prompt: Azure's Elastic Database tools use a specific database to track which range of a sharding key lives on which shard, so a client library can route each query to the correct shard automatically. What is that component called?
options: The shard map manager — a database that tracks which sharding-key range lives on which shard, letting the client library route queries automatically
The split-merge service — a database that stores a full copy of every shard's data for failover purposes
An elastic pool — a shared compute budget that also tracks which shard holds which customer range
A linked server — a server-level object that lets one shard query another shard's tables directly
questions.explain: The shard map manager is the specific database that tracks which sharding-key range (like a CustomerID range) lives on which shard, so an application can ask it "where does this key live" and get routed straight there. The split-merge service is a different component — it physically moves ranges of data between shards to rebalance them, it doesn't track the map itself. Elastic pools and linked servers solve unrelated problems entirely.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 14's deployment-decision framework in the correct order.
items: Default to Azure SQL Database as the starting point for any new workload
Escalate to Azure SQL Managed Instance only if a specific requirement forces it — SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries, linked servers, CLR, or Service Broker
Escalate further to SQL Server on an Azure VM only if a specific requirement forces it — OS-level access, an unsupported version or feature, or direct control of the patching cadence
Stop escalating the moment the current tier satisfies every real requirement — most workloads never need to leave Azure SQL Database
questions.explain: Lesson 14's framework moves to the next tier only when a specific, named requirement forces it, never on "might be nice to have." You start at Azure SQL Database, check whether a real requirement forces Managed Instance, check whether a further requirement forces a VM, and stop the moment nothing on the next tier's list actually applies — which is why most new workloads never leave Azure SQL Database at all.

questions.prompt: A user is a member of db_datareader, which grants SELECT on every table in the database, but also has an explicit DENY SELECT on Sales.SalaryDetails specifically. Which statement correctly describes what happens when that user tries to SELECT from Sales.SalaryDetails, and how REVOKE would differ from both GRANT and DENY here?
options: The explicit DENY blocks SELECT on Sales.SalaryDetails regardless of the db_datareader grant, because DENY overrides every GRANT from any source; REVOKE would only remove an explicit statement, not grant or deny anything by itself
The db_datareader grant wins because role-based permissions always override individual object-level statements; REVOKE would reverse the DENY into a GRANT
SQL Server raises an error the moment a GRANT and a DENY conflict on the same object, requiring the DBA to remove one before any query against that table can run
The DENY only blocks SELECT for SQL-authenticated logins, not for users mapped through Microsoft Entra authentication, so an Entra-authenticated member of db_datareader could still read the table
Whichever statement — the role membership or the DENY — was issued most recently takes effect, regardless of which one it is
REVOKE SELECT would need to be run twice, once against the GRANT and once against the DENY, before the user could read any other table in the database
questions.explain: DENY is an explicit block that overrides every other path to a permission, including role membership — db_datareader's broad SELECT grant loses to the specific DENY on Sales.SalaryDetails, full stop. REVOKE is neither GRANT nor DENY's opposite: it simply removes one explicit statement and reveals whatever other path remains, so REVOKE DENY SELECT here would remove the deny and leave db_datareader's grant intact, not flip anything.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets the precedence exactly backwards — DENY beats GRANT regardless of whether that GRANT comes from a direct statement or from role membership like db_datareader; role membership never overrides an explicit DENY. REVOKE also never turns a DENY into a GRANT — it only erases the one explicit statement it targets, leaving whatever other path (like the role membership) still in effect underneath it.

questions.prompt: An organization disables an employee's account in Microsoft Entra ID. That employee had Entra-authenticated access to twelve different Azure SQL databases, each created with CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER. What happens to their database access, and why?
options: Access to all twelve databases stops immediately, because each Entra-authenticated user is only a reference to the identity in Entra ID — disabling it there removes the credential everywhere at once
Access continues until an administrator also runs DROP USER in each of the twelve databases individually, since CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER stores its own password copy inside SQL Server
Access stops only for databases on the logical server where the Microsoft Entra admin was originally configured; the other eleven databases keep working
Nothing changes right away, because SQL Server caches Entra credentials locally for a fixed period regardless of the Entra ID account's status
questions.explain: FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER means the identity isn't stored in SQL Server at all — it's a reference to an identity that exists in Entra ID. That's exactly the centralized-management advantage Lesson 19 names: disable the person in Entra ID once, and every Entra-authenticated login they had, across every database, stops working immediately, with no per-database cleanup required — the opposite of SQL authentication's one-password-per-system problem.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about authentication and authorization in Azure SQL, per Chapter 4.
options: A login answers whether an identity can connect to the server at all; a user answers what that identity can do inside one specific database
The same login can map to users with different names and different rights in different databases on the same server
CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER requires a separate CREATE LOGIN statement first, the same way SQL authentication does
A Microsoft Entra admin has to be set on the logical server before any CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER statement can succeed in a database on that server
sysadmin is a fixed database role that grants full control of exactly one specific database
questions.explain: A login is a server-level object answering "can this connect at all"; a user is database-level, answering "what can it do in this one database" — and the same login genuinely can map to differently-named, differently-privileged users across different databases on the same server. Entra authentication skips CREATE LOGIN entirely — CREATE USER ... FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER is both the reference and the grant point in one statement, which is only possible after a Microsoft Entra admin is configured on the logical server. sysadmin is a fixed server role covering the entire server, not a database role scoped to one database.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: granting db_owner to a service account just to make "the app can't read this table" go away is a common anti-pattern because it hands over far more than was ever needed; the correct discipline instead — starting from nothing and adding only proven-necessary permissions — is called the principle of ________.
questions.explain: Least privilege means an account starts with no access and gains only the specific permissions it's been shown to need, nothing granted "to be safe." The db_owner shortcut fixes one missing SELECT by handing out full control of the entire database — the ability to drop tables and change every other account's permissions — which is exactly the anti-pattern Lesson 24 names.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 30's Azure SQL connectivity troubleshooting checklist in the correct order.
items: Confirm whether the symptom is cannot-connect, login-failed, or connects-but-slow
Check server-level and database-level firewall rules against the client's actual current public IP
Confirm the VNet service endpoint, the server-side Virtual Network rule, and any NSGs all allow the specific subnet
If using a Private Endpoint, confirm DNS resolves the server name to the private IP via the privatelink.database.windows.net zone
Confirm the client driver and the server's minimum TLS version setting are actually compatible
questions.explain: Lesson 30's checklist is ordered from earliest in the connection path to latest: first classify the symptom (network vs. login vs. performance), then firewall rules, then VNet/NSG rules, then DNS resolution for Private Link, and only then TLS version compatibility. Checking a later layer before an earlier one wastes time — there's no point debugging TLS if the firewall rejected the packet before TLS negotiation ever started.

questions.prompt: A compliance requirement states the production database must have no public network path at all, not merely one restricted by firewall rules. A DBA responds by enabling a VNet service endpoint on the app's subnet and narrowing the server's firewall to allow only that subnet's traffic. Does this configuration satisfy the requirement?
options: No — the server still has a public, DNS-resolvable endpoint; a service endpoint only tags which traffic is allowed through that endpoint, it doesn't remove the public endpoint itself
Yes — once a Virtual Network rule is the only allowed traffic source, the public endpoint is effectively disabled
No — service endpoints only work for Managed Instance, not Azure SQL Database, so this configuration doesn't apply here at all
Yes — a service endpoint's traffic is private by definition, so it never touches Azure SQL's public endpoint
questions.explain: Per Lesson 29's decision framework, a firewall rule or VNet service endpoint is a 'gated public' posture, not a 'no public exposure' posture — the public DNS name and IP still exist and are still technically reachable from the internet, just narrowed by rules. A compliance requirement that explicitly says 'no public network path' needs a Private Endpoint (Lesson 28), which removes the public path for that traffic entirely instead of merely gating it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Private Endpoint's private IP only resolves correctly for clients when the Azure Private DNS zone named ________ is linked to the consuming VNet, with a record pointing the server's name at the new private IP.
questions.explain: Lesson 28 and Lesson 30 both flag this as the part that quietly breaks private connectivity: without the privatelink.database.windows.net zone linked to the VNet, clients keep resolving the server's name to its public IP, either bypassing the private path entirely or failing outright if public access is also disabled.

questions.prompt: A healthcare company needs a column-level control where even a user holding full SELECT permission on the table — including a sysadmin-level DBA, or someone who restored a stolen backup elsewhere — can never retrieve a patient SSN column's real plaintext value by querying it, no matter how the query is phrased. Which control, on its own, actually guarantees this?
options: Always Encrypted, since SQL Server itself never holds the Column Encryption Key or sees the plaintext
Dynamic Data Masking, with the UNMASK permission denied to that user
Transparent Data Encryption (TDE), since the column's data is encrypted on disk
Row-Level Security with a FILTER predicate restricting which rows that user can see
SQL Auditing scoped to log every SELECT against that column
Data Discovery & Classification labeling the column Highly Confidential
questions.explain: Always Encrypted's defining property is that SQL Server itself never has the key and never sees the plaintext for that column — encryption and decryption happen client-side using a Column Master Key stored outside the database entirely. That means even a sysadmin with full SELECT, or someone who restored a stolen backup elsewhere, cannot read the real value without separately obtaining the Column Master Key. Every other option still lets a sufficiently privileged user see the real value through SQL Server itself.
questions.distractorExplain: Dynamic Data Masking looks like a strong fit because it also hides values regardless of other permissions like db_owner — but Lesson 33 is explicit that DDM is a least-exposure convenience control, not a real security boundary: a user with enough query access can still filter on the real value in a WHERE clause or work around the mask some other way, because the data was never actually encrypted or hidden from SQL Server itself, just reformatted in the result set. A determined, permitted user — which is exactly what the question describes — can defeat DDM; they cannot defeat Always Encrypted.

questions.prompt: A sales rep successfully runs an INSERT into Orders claiming a SalesRepID that belongs to a different rep. The row goes in with no error, but it never shows up later when that same rep runs SELECT * FROM Orders. What does this indicate about the Row-Level Security policy on this table?
options: Only a FILTER predicate is configured — it silently hides non-matching rows on SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE, but a FILTER predicate alone doesn't stop a mismatched INSERT; a BLOCK predicate is needed to reject that insert outright
The predicate function is missing SCHEMABINDING, so RLS isn't enforcing anything at all on this table
RLS only ever applies to SELECT statements, so INSERT was never going to be restricted regardless of which predicate type is configured
The security policy's STATE is set to OFF, which happens to permit inserts while still filtering selects
questions.explain: Lesson 34 draws exactly this distinction: a FILTER predicate applies to SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE, silently narrowing what's visible or affected — but it doesn't actively reject a write. Preventing an INSERT that claims a mismatched SalesRepID requires a BLOCK predicate, which throws an error instead of silently filtering. The symptom described — a clean insert that's simply invisible afterward — is the textbook sign that only FILTER, not BLOCK, is in place.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Ledger, Change Tracking, and SQL Auditing, per Lesson 37.
options: Ledger can cryptographically prove a table's history hasn't been altered, even by someone with sysadmin rights
Change Tracking keeps a full history of every value a row has ever held, which is exactly why it's suitable for a compliance investigation
SQL Auditing records who did what and when, but by itself can't cryptographically prove the stored audit log wasn't later altered
Change Tracking answers 'which rows changed since I last checked,' for synchronization scenarios, and isn't a security or compliance feature
Ledger and SQL Auditing answer the exact same question, so a database realistically only needs one of them enabled
questions.explain: Ledger computes a cryptographic digest you can store outside the database and later use to verify history wasn't tampered with — a stronger guarantee than logging alone, which is exactly what sets it apart from auditing. SQL Auditing records a historical log of who did what, but that log itself, sitting in Storage or Log Analytics, has no built-in cryptographic proof against later tampering — that's the specific gap Ledger closes. Change Tracking is explicitly lightweight: it tracks which rows changed for sync scenarios, keeps no full value history, and isn't a security or compliance tool at all. Auditing answers 'who did what and when'; Ledger answers 'can I prove this history is genuine' — two different questions, not the same one twice.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 6 control to the specific question it actually answers.
right: Can I cryptographically prove this table's history wasn't tampered with, even by a sysadmin?
What should an unprivileged user see in the result set, without changing any stored data?
Who accessed this table, and when, recorded outside the audited database itself?
Which rows is this specific session even allowed to see or affect, based on a predicate?
questions.explain: Dynamic Data Masking rewrites what an unprivileged user sees in query results without touching stored data. Row-Level Security restricts which rows a session can see or affect at all, below the object-permission layer. SQL Auditing produces a historical record of who accessed what, written to a destination outside the audited database. Ledger goes further than auditing by cryptographically proving that recorded history is genuine and untampered.

questions.prompt: You manage 80 Azure SQL databases spread across several subscriptions in the same Microsoft Entra tenant, and you want one dashboard answering 'which of my databases needs attention right now' instead of opening each database's own Azure Monitor blade one at a time. Which tool from Chapter 7 actually fits this need?
options: Database Watcher — it's built specifically to register many SQL targets and centralize their monitoring data into one estate-wide view
Azure Monitor alert rules — stacking enough individual alert rules together produces the same fleet-wide view
sys.dm_db_resource_stats — query it against each database in a loop to manually build the same view yourself
Extended Events — a single session can be pointed at every database across a tenant at once
questions.explain: Lesson 40 is explicit about the gap Database Watcher fills: Azure Monitor and the DMVs are built around one resource at a time, which falls apart once you're responsible for dozens or hundreds of databases. A watcher registers up to 100 SQL targets, even across subscriptions within the same Entra tenant, and centralizes their data into estate-level dashboards (like a fleet-wide CPU heatmap) exactly to answer 'which database needs attention now' as a single question.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about building a performance baseline, per Lesson 38.
options: A baseline should be captured over at least a full business cycle, not a single quiet day, so it reflects normal variation rather than a lucky Tuesday
Averages alone are sufficient for query duration, since percentiles mostly duplicate what the average already shows
Wait statistics belong in a real baseline because they reveal what kind of bottleneck — I/O, CPU, or blocking — is normal for this specific database
A baseline should be re-established after a workload change, such as a new feature shipping or a marketing campaign doubling traffic
Once established, a baseline never needs to be revisited, since normal usage patterns don't meaningfully change over time
questions.explain: A real baseline is captured over at least a full business cycle, including a known-heavy period, precisely so it reflects genuine normal variation. Wait statistics tell you what kind of bottleneck is normal for this database before you're troubleshooting one under pressure. A baseline goes stale the moment the underlying workload changes, so it should be re-established after events like a new feature or a traffic spike — and even without an obvious trigger, a baseline older than a quarter is worth treating with suspicion. Percentiles, not averages, are what matter for query duration, because an average can hide a slow tail that a handful of outlier executions create — the exact opposite of option B's claim.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 7 monitoring tool or DMV to what it actually reports.
right: Cumulative wait time by wait type, accumulated since the last restart or manual reset
Where a captured XEvents session's data is actually written — a ring buffer in memory, or an .xel file on disk
One row per authenticated session, showing login name, host, and resource usage since that session connected
An Azure SQL-only view returning roughly the last hour of CPU, I/O, and memory history, sampled every 15 seconds
questions.explain: sys.dm_exec_sessions is one row per authenticated session with login, host, and resource-usage detail since connect. sys.dm_db_resource_stats is Azure SQL-specific, sampling CPU/IO/memory every 15 seconds for roughly the last hour. sys.dm_os_wait_stats accumulates wait time by wait type since the last restart. An Extended Events target is simply where a session's captured events land — a ring buffer or an event file — distinct from what any single DMV reports.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the ________ DMV is specific to Azure SQL Database and returns one row every 15 seconds, covering roughly the last hour of CPU, I/O, and memory utilization history — straight T-SQL, with no Azure Monitor setup required.
questions.explain: sys.dm_db_resource_stats doesn't exist on on-prem SQL Server, because on-prem has no provisioned-tier concept to report utilization against. It gives you exactly the resource-consumption side of a Lesson 38 baseline without needing Azure Monitor at all.

questions.prompt: This query's execution plan shows an Index Seek against IX_SalesOrderHeader_CustomerID, followed by a Key Lookup before TotalDue is returned. Which option most accurately explains what's happening and the most direct fix?
options: The nonclustered index on CustomerID doesn't store TotalDue, so SQL Server makes a second trip to the clustered index per matching row; adding TotalDue as an included column makes it a covering index and removes the lookup
The Key Lookup means the table has no clustered index at all, so SQL Server is scanning a heap using a RID Lookup instead
The Key Lookup indicates the CustomerID predicate is non-SARGable and needs to be rewritten to avoid a function call
The Key Lookup means the optimizer chose a Hash Match instead of Nested Loops for this query, and a join hint will remove it
The Key Lookup is unavoidable overhead that no index design can ever eliminate, so it should simply be ignored
The Key Lookup means statistics on CustomerID are stale and will disappear once UPDATE STATISTICS is run
questions.explain: A nonclustered index only stores its key columns plus a pointer back to the full row. Since IX_SalesOrderHeader_CustomerID doesn't cover TotalDue, SQL Server performs a Key Lookup back to the clustered index for every matching row to fetch it. Lesson 46 is explicit that the fix is adding the missing column as an INCLUDE, turning the index into a covering index and eliminating the extra trip entirely — exactly the kind of fix SSMS's own missing-index suggestion (Lesson 47) would surface.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it names a real, related operator — but the plan specifically names a Key Lookup, not a RID Lookup. Lesson 46 draws that exact distinction: a Key Lookup goes back to a clustered index, while a RID Lookup is what happens against a heap with no clustered index at all. The query already has a clustered table (implied by the Key Lookup terminology itself), so claiming there's no clustered index contradicts the very operator named in the question.

questions.prompt: A DBA sees one query running slowly and immediately creates a new index on it, without first checking wait statistics. Afterward, this query shows PAGEIOLATCH_SH as the top wait by a wide margin, and it had been the top wait the whole time. What does this actually reveal?
options: The real bottleneck was disk I/O, not a missing index — the new index likely didn't address the actual cause of the slowdown
PAGEIOLATCH_SH confirms the missing index was exactly the right fix, since page I/O latches are released once an index covers the query
PAGEIOLATCH_SH means the query was being blocked by another session, and the index change was irrelevant to that blocking either way
PAGEIOLATCH_SH only appears after an index is added, so this result couldn't have existed before the DBA made the change
questions.explain: Lesson 44 is explicit that the single most common troubleshooting mistake is guessing at a fix — usually 'add an index' — before confirming what SQL Server is actually waiting on. PAGEIOLATCH_SH specifically points to disk I/O as the bottleneck, not a missing index; an LCK_M_* wait would have pointed to blocking instead. Creating an index without checking this first risks spending real effort on a change that was never going to fix the actual cause.

questions.code:
ALTER DATABASE CURRENT
SET AUTOMATIC_TUNING (FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN = ON);
questions.prompt: This setting is enabled on a database. A brand-new report query — one that has never executed before — runs with a poor plan from its very first execution. Will Automatic Tuning fix this on its own?
options: No — Automatic Tuning forces a previously known-good plan for a detected regression; a query with no execution history has no earlier good plan to fall back to
Yes — Automatic Tuning builds an optimal plan for any new query the first time it runs, regardless of whether it has history
No — Automatic Tuning only applies to Managed Instance, and never to Azure SQL Database
Yes — FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN also retroactively applies Intelligent Query Processing features to any query lacking history
questions.explain: Lesson 52 is explicit that Automatic Tuning won't catch every regression, specifically calling out that a genuinely new query has no 'last good plan' to fall back to. It detects a statistically significant regression against a query's own Query Store history and forces the earlier known-good plan — a brand-new query simply has no earlier plan for it to force.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Intelligent Query Processing (IQP), per Lesson 52.
options: Batch Mode on Rowstore can process rows in batches even for a plain rowstore table, not only for columnstore tables
Memory Grant Feedback adjusts a query's memory grant on its NEXT execution, based on what the previous execution actually used
Adaptive Joins choose between Nested Loops and Hash Join before the query runs, based purely on the optimizer's upfront row-count estimate
IQP features require a DBA to explicitly enable each one individually, beyond having a current-enough database compatibility level
IQP corrects course based on what actually happens during execution, rather than relying only on the optimizer's pre-execution estimate
questions.explain: Batch Mode on Rowstore applies even to plain rowstore tables, not just columnstore. Memory Grant Feedback specifically adjusts the NEXT execution's grant based on the prior execution's actual usage. Adaptive Joins pick between Nested Loops and Hash Join AFTER seeing the actual row count, not before — the opposite of option C's claim. None of these require a DBA to enable anything special beyond a current-enough compatibility level, contradicting option D. Overall, IQP's defining trait is correcting a bad upfront estimate using what actually happened at runtime.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Query Store, per Lessons 48-49.
options: Query Store persists query text, plans, and runtime statistics to disk, surviving a restart — unlike sys.dm_exec_query_stats
On Azure SQL Database, Query Store must be manually turned on with ALTER DATABASE before it captures anything
Forcing a plan with sp_query_store_force_plan is a stabilizer that buys time, not a permanent substitute for diagnosing the real cause
The Compare Plans feature lays two plan IDs for the same query side by side and highlights which operators actually changed between them
QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO captures every single ad hoc query that ever runs, specifically so nothing is ever missed
questions.explain: Query Store persists query text, every plan a query has used, and runtime statistics to disk across restarts — exactly what DMVs like sys.dm_exec_query_stats don't survive. Forcing a plan is explicitly described as a stabilizer, buying time while the real cause gets diagnosed, not a permanent fix. Compare Plans lays two plan IDs side by side and highlights the differing operators automatically. Query Store is on by default on Azure SQL Database, contradicting option B, and QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO deliberately skips one-off ad hoc queries to reduce noise, the opposite of option E's claim.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 44's performance troubleshooting methodology in the correct order.
items: Scope the problem: is it one specific query, or is the whole system affected?
Determine timing: is this a new regression, or has the query always been this slow?
Check wait statistics first — instance-wide or for the specific session — before touching any query or index
Only then read the execution plan, audit index health, or consult Query Store, guided by what the wait type pointed to
questions.explain: Lesson 44's methodology is deliberately ordered: scope the problem first (one query vs. the whole instance), then establish timing (new regression vs. always slow), then check wait statistics before touching anything, and only then reach for execution plans, index DMVs, or Query Store — with the wait type telling you which of those tools actually applies. Skipping straight to an execution plan or an index change before checking waits is the single most expensive mistake this lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: A DBA runs sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats and finds two indexes: one with 280 pages at 85% fragmentation, and one with 60,000 pages at 25% fragmentation. Per Lesson 53's guidance on measuring and fixing fragmentation, which pair of actions is most appropriate?
options: Leave the 280-page index alone, since it's too small for fragmentation to cost real I/O either way; reorganize the 60,000-page index, since 25% falls within the typical reorganize band
Rebuild both indexes immediately, since any fragmentation above 20% should always be rebuilt regardless of index size
Reorganize the 280-page index to fix its 85% fragmentation; leave the 60,000-page index alone since 25% is within acceptable limits
Rebuild the 280-page index since 85% exceeds the rebuild threshold; ignore the 60,000-page index since REORGANIZE only applies to small indexes
Run UPDATE STATISTICS WITH FULLSCAN on both indexes instead of REBUILD or REORGANIZE, since statistics maintenance addresses fragmentation directly
Reorganize both indexes, since REORGANIZE is always the safer, lower-risk choice regardless of fragmentation percentage or index size
questions.explain: Lesson 53 is explicit that the page_count filter matters as much as the fragmentation percentage: a small index like the 280-page one fits in a handful of reads regardless of how fragmented it looks, so fixing it buys nothing. The 60,000-page index is large enough that physical layout genuinely determines scan cost, and 25% sits inside the common 5-30% reorganize band rather than the 30%+ rebuild band.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D correctly reasons from a fragmentation-percentage threshold, which is the right instinct — but it applies that threshold to the wrong index and gets the page_count rule backwards. It targets the 280-page index for a rebuild even though an index that small was never worth touching in the first place, and it treats REORGANIZE as something that 'only applies to small indexes,' when Lesson 53 actually says the opposite: REORGANIZE's lighter footprint is often the better choice specifically on large, hot tables where a REBUILD's resource spike is unaffordable.

questions.prompt: A DBA wants to cap a reporting login's workload at 30% CPU on an instance that also serves OLTP traffic, using Resource Governor's resource pool and classifier function approach. The database in question is on Azure SQL Database. What should the DBA conclude, per Lesson 57?
options: Resource Governor can be configured directly on Azure SQL Database, since it's a core SQL Server engine feature available identically on every deployment model
Resource Governor isn't available on Azure SQL Database at all — Azure SQL Database enforces per-database resource ceilings through its own service-tier (DTU/vCore) limits instead
Resource Governor is available on Azure SQL Database, but only through the classifier function, without resource pools or workload groups
The DBA must migrate to Azure SQL Managed Instance first, since Resource Governor cannot be configured on any Azure deployment model at all
questions.explain: Resource Governor is an instance-level SQL Server engine feature, available on SQL Server on an Azure VM and on Azure SQL Managed Instance — anywhere with instance-level control. Azure SQL Database has no instance-level surface and doesn't expose Resource Governor; it solves the same noisy-neighbor problem a different way, through its own platform-enforced DTU/vCore ceilings per database.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about statistics maintenance, per Lesson 54.
options: Auto-update statistics is reactive — it fires only after enough rows have changed, so some queries run against stale statistics before the threshold is even reached
With AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS_ASYNC ON, the query that actually triggers the statistics refresh still runs against the old, stale statistics while the refresh happens in the background
DBCC SHOW_STATISTICS ... WITH STAT_HEADER's Updated column is the fastest way to confirm whether a bad plan is a statistics problem before looking anywhere else
Stale statistics can only make the optimizer choose a slightly slower plan — never an entirely wrong shape of plan
UPDATE STATISTICS ... WITH FULLSCAN samples a representative subset of rows for speed, the same way the default auto-update behavior does
questions.explain: Auto-update only fires after a change threshold accumulates, so queries run on stale statistics in the meantime, and ASYNC mode means even the triggering query doesn't wait for the fresh statistics. STAT_HEADER's Updated column is exactly the fast first check Lesson 54 recommends. Stale statistics can make the optimizer pick the wrong shape of plan entirely — not just a slower one — because a bad cardinality estimate can swing the choice between, say, a nested loop and a hash join. FULLSCAN is the opposite of sampling: it reads every row, which is exactly why it's expensive but exact.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 55, when DBCC CHECKDB finds corruption and there's no good backup to restore from, put these steps of the last-resort repair process in the correct order.
items: Run DBCC CHECKDB WITH NO_INFOMSGS, ALL_ERRORMSGS to diagnose without making any changes
Put the database into single-user mode with ALTER DATABASE ... SET SINGLE_USER WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE
Run DBCC CHECKDB with the REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS option as the genuine last resort
Return the database to multi-user mode with ALTER DATABASE ... SET MULTI_USER
questions.explain: Lesson 55's process diagnoses first without making changes, so you know what you're dealing with. REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS requires exclusive access to make structural changes safely, which is why single-user mode comes next. The repair itself runs third, and only after it completes does the database return to multi-user mode so applications can reconnect. Restoring from a known-good backup should always be tried before any of this — repair makes the database consistent, not complete, and whatever it deletes is gone for good.

questions.prompt: A team asks you to "set up a SQL Server Agent job" on an Azure SQL Database (not Managed Instance, not a VM). Per Lesson 59, what's the accurate answer?
options: Agent works identically on Azure SQL Database as it does on a VM or Managed Instance, so proceed with sp_add_job as usual

Traditional SQL Server Agent isn't available on Azure SQL Database, because it's an instance-level service and Azure SQL Database has no instance-level surface — use Elastic Database Jobs (or Azure Automation) instead
Agent is available on Azure SQL Database, but only for T-SQL steps, never PowerShell or CmdExec steps
Agent is available on Azure SQL Database only if the database is part of an elastic pool with at least two other databases
questions.explain: Lesson 59 is direct about this: Azure SQL Database's exclusion of traditional Agent isn't a missing feature, it's structural. Azure SQL Database is a single-database PaaS product with no instance-level surface, and Agent is fundamentally an instance-level service. The real equivalent on that platform is Elastic Database Jobs (Lesson 68), not a workaround within Agent itself.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SQL Server Agent job steps and schedules, per Lesson 60.
options: A job step's on-success action and on-fail action are configured independently of each other
sp_add_jobserver with no @server_name targets the local server, and skipping this step entirely means the job never actually runs anywhere
A single job can mix step types — TSQL, PowerShell, CmdExec, and SSIS steps can all appear inside the same job
A schedule is attached directly to each individual step, not to the job as a whole
sp_attach_schedule is a separate step from sp_add_schedule specifically because a single schedule object can only ever be used by one job at a time
questions.explain: On-success and on-fail actions are set per step, independently, which is exactly what makes deliberate failure paths possible. Forgetting sp_add_jobserver leaves a job with no server target, so it never runs. Agent steps genuinely mix subsystems — TSQL, PowerShell, CmdExec, SSIS — inside one job. A schedule attaches to the whole job, not to individual steps, and sp_attach_schedule is a separate call specifically because one schedule object CAN be reused across several different jobs, not because it's restricted to one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 61, SQL Server Agent alerts on error severity ________ and above are the real, meaningful threshold Microsoft treats as requiring immediate DBA attention, not "log it and check later."
questions.explain: Lesson 61 calls out severity 19 and above specifically: these are resource errors and internal-consistency errors serious enough that Microsoft's own documentation treats them as requiring immediate attention, which is why a production maintenance strategy wires a severity-based alert at that threshold rather than relying only on job-failure notifications.

questions.prompt: Match each SQL Server Agent object type to what it actually is, per Lesson 59.
right: The record of every run, per step, with success/failure status and duration
A named, schedulable container made of one or more steps
When the job runs — attached to the job as a whole, not to individual steps
One action inside a job, such as a T-SQL, PowerShell, CmdExec, or SSIS task
questions.explain: A Job is the named container; a Job Step is one piece of work inside it with its own type and on-failure behavior; a Schedule is attached to the job as a whole and triggers the whole thing; Job History is the automatic record of every run, written per step, which is the first place Lesson 62 says to look when a job didn't do what it was supposed to.

questions.prompt: A company runs 40 databases in an Azure SQL Database elastic pool and needs the same index-maintenance stored procedure to run on a weekly schedule across all 40, with new databases added to the pool later picked up automatically. Per Lesson 68, what's the right tool, and why?
options: SQL Server Agent, because an Agent job's @target_group_name parameter can point directly at an entire elastic pool

Elastic Jobs, because its job agent database stores the schedule and script once, and a target group lets that single job run against every database in the group, including ones added to the group later
Azure Automation runbooks are required, since neither Agent nor Elastic Jobs can run a T-SQL script against more than one database at a time
ARM templates, since infrastructure as code is the correct way to repeat the same maintenance task across many databases
questions.explain: Lesson 68 is specific: a job agent database stores the job's definition, schedule, and history, a target group is the named set of databases the job runs against, and adding a new database to that target group later means the existing weekly job runs against it automatically — no change to the job definition needed. SQL Server Agent isn't the tool here at all, since Azure SQL Database doesn't support it as a full on-server scheduler (Lesson 59).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 68, the ________ is the small, dedicated database that stores an elastic job's definitions, schedules, and execution history — it doesn't hold your application's actual data.
questions.explain: Elastic Jobs has three pieces: the job agent database (automation metadata only, not application data), the target group (which databases the job runs against), and the job itself (the T-SQL script plus a schedule).

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 69, put these troubleshooting steps for a failed automated database deployment in the correct order.
items: Check the pipeline log first, not the database
Confirm the identity the pipeline is running as, such as a service principal or managed identity
Re-run the exact same command manually, with the same parameters, to isolate pipeline problems from deployment problems
questions.explain: Lesson 69's order starts with the pipeline log, because a failed deployment often means the pipeline's own plumbing broke — authentication or a parameter typo — while the database itself may be fine. Next, confirm the identity the pipeline authenticates as, since a service principal or managed identity often has narrower rights than the DBA's own login, causing permission errors that never show up when run manually. Re-running the identical command by hand comes last specifically because it isolates whether the real problem is the pipeline's environment or the deployment itself.

questions.prompt: A team picks Azure SQL Database as their migration target first, because it's the cheapest option, and only discovers mid-migration that one database depends on a linked server. Per Lesson 70, what planning mistake did they make?
options: They should have picked Managed Instance from the start, since it's always the safer default target for any migration
They picked a target before completing the inventory and defining success criteria — the correct order is inventory first, then success criteria, then target
They should have skipped the inventory step entirely and relied only on the Data Migration Assistant's report
They made no real planning mistake, since linked server dependencies can always be resolved after cutover with no redesign
questions.explain: Lesson 70 lays out the planning order deliberately: inventory everything first, including dependencies like linked servers, then define concrete success criteria, and only then pick a target. Picking the target first — specifically because it looked cheapest — is called out as the most common planning mistake, since the right target depends entirely on what the inventory and success criteria turn up.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about migration assessment, per Lesson 71.
options: A compatibility issue is a blocking problem that prevents a clean migration until it's fixed
A feature parity gap means a capability simply doesn't exist on the target, without necessarily blocking the migration itself
Cross-database queries not existing in Azure SQL Database is a compatibility issue, the same category as a blocking migration error
Sizing a target's compute/storage tier should be based on peak CPU and memory utilization on the source, not average utilization
Compatibility issues and feature parity gaps should be treated identically during planning, since both block migration the same way
questions.explain: A compatibility issue blocks the migration until fixed; a feature parity gap is a capability that just doesn't travel with it, without blocking the move itself. Lesson 71 names cross-database queries not existing in Azure SQL Database as exactly this second category, a parity gap, not a compatibility break. Sizing deliberately uses peak CPU/memory, not average, because average hides the actual bottleneck moment. Treating the two categories the same is called out directly as a mistake, since a parity gap might just mean redesigning one feature, while a compatibility issue genuinely blocks the move.

questions.prompt: Match each migration concept to what it actually is, per Lessons 73 and 74.
right: Does not support RESTORE DATABASE ... FROM URL; the real migration path is BACPAC export/import or DMS instead
Supports native RESTORE DATABASE ... FROM URL straight from an on-prem backup, because of much higher feature parity with on-prem SQL Server
A portable package containing schema and data, exported from the source and imported with az sql db import
Microsoft's managed service that handles continuous sync from an on-prem source into Azure SQL Database with a short final cutover
questions.explain: Azure SQL Database can't use native RESTORE FROM URL at all; its real paths are BACPAC import for an offline move or DMS for an online, continuously-synced one. Managed Instance's much higher feature parity with on-prem SQL Server is exactly what makes native RESTORE ... FROM URL work there directly from an on-prem backup. A BACPAC is the portable schema-and-data package that path relies on, and DMS is Microsoft's purpose-built service for the online version of that same move.

questions.prompt: After cutting over to Azure SQL Managed Instance, an application's service account that worked fine against the old on-prem server now fails to authenticate against the new target, even though SSMS can connect fine with a different login. Per Lesson 75, what's the most likely cause?
options: A collation mismatch between source and target is causing the login to fail
The service account's SQL login on the source was never recreated as a contained user on the target, so authentication fails specifically against the new server
Row counts don't match between source and target, which by itself causes login failures
Query performance is worse on the new target, and SQL Server reports that as a login error
questions.explain: Lesson 75 calls this out as one of the common post-cutover failure patterns: SQL logins don't migrate automatically, so if a login-to-user mapping was missed, that service account authenticates fine against the old server and fails against the new one. A collation mismatch causes subtly wrong comparisons and joins, not login failures; row-count mismatches and slower queries are separate validation concerns entirely unrelated to authentication.

questions.prompt: A database has a full backup from Sunday 2am, a differential backup from Wednesday 2am, and hourly transaction log backups since Wednesday 2am. A DBA needs to restore the database to Thursday 10am. Which restore sequence correctly does this?
options: Restore the Sunday full backup WITH NORECOVERY, restore the Wednesday differential WITH NORECOVERY, then restore every hourly log backup from immediately after the differential through 10am Thursday, applying WITH RECOVERY only on the final log backup
Restore only the most recent hourly log backup taken before 10am Thursday WITH RECOVERY, since it is the most recent backup available
Restore the Wednesday differential WITH RECOVERY first, then restore the Sunday full backup WITH NORECOVERY, then apply the log backups
Restore the Sunday full backup WITH RECOVERY, then the Wednesday differential WITH RECOVERY, skipping the log backups since the differential already contains the changes made since Sunday
Restore every hourly log backup since Wednesday WITH NORECOVERY first, then restore the Sunday full backup WITH RECOVERY to apply it as the base

Restore the Wednesday differential WITH NORECOVERY, then restore the Sunday full backup WITH NORECOVERY, then apply the logs, since the differential already contains most of the data, order between full and differential doesn't matter
questions.explain: A restore always rebuilds the chain in order: the last full backup, then the most recent differential taken after it, then every log backup in sequence from immediately after that differential up through the target time. WITH NORECOVERY keeps the database in a restoring state so the next backup in the chain can still be applied; only the very last restore step in the whole sequence uses WITH RECOVERY to bring the database online.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D restores the full backup and differential in the correct order, but using WITH RECOVERY on the full backup brings the database online immediately and rolls back any uncommitted work, which ends the restore sequence right there. Once a step uses RECOVERY, no further backup — differential or log — can be layered on top, so the differential and every log backup after it become unusable, and the restore can never reach Thursday 10am.

questions.code:
RESTORE DATABASE Sales
FROM DISK = 'D:\Backups\Sales_Full.bak'
WITH RECOVERY;

-- next step, intended to apply a differential on top:
RESTORE DATABASE Sales
FROM DISK = 'D:\Backups\Sales_Diff.bak'
WITH NORECOVERY;
questions.prompt: A DBA runs this sequence, intending to restore the full backup and then apply a differential on top of it. What actually happens?
options: The second RESTORE fails — the first statement's WITH RECOVERY already brought the database online and rolled back uncommitted transactions, so no further backup can be applied on top of it
Both statements succeed normally — WITH RECOVERY only affects transaction log restores, not full database restores, so the differential still applies cleanly
SQL Server silently ignores the WITH RECOVERY clause on the first statement, since it detects a differential restore is coming next
The first RESTORE fails outright, because WITH RECOVERY is not a valid option on a RESTORE DATABASE statement for a full backup
questions.explain: WITH RECOVERY rolls back uncommitted transactions and brings the database online, ending the restore sequence — this applies to a full-backup restore exactly the same as a log restore. Once that happens, there is no restoring-state database left to apply the differential to. Every restore step in a chain needs WITH NORECOVERY except the last one.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure SQL Database's point-in-time restore and long-term retention (LTR), as covered in Lessons 79-80.
options: Both a point-in-time restore and an LTR restore create a brand-new database rather than overwriting the original
The short-term point-in-time restore window defaults to 7 days and can be configured up to 35 days
An LTR policy can retain designated weekly, monthly, or yearly full backups for up to 10 years, independent of the short-term retention window
A deleted Azure SQL Database is restored from the database's own (now-deleted) Overview page, the same way an existing database is restored
An LTR restore lets you pick any exact second within its retention period, with the same precision as a point-in-time restore
questions.explain: Both restore types create a new database alongside the original rather than overwriting anything. The short-term window defaults to 7 days, configurable up to 35. LTR is a separate policy retaining designated full backups for up to 10 years. A deleted database has no Overview page left to restore from — it's restored from the server's 'Deleted databases' list instead. An LTR restore gives you the specific full backups the policy designated, not an arbitrary timestamp — that precision belongs to point-in-time restore alone.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: to back up an on-prem or Azure VM-hosted SQL Server directly to Azure Blob Storage instead of a local disk, a DBA replaces TO DISK with ________ in the BACKUP DATABASE statement, after first creating a credential that lets SQL Server authenticate to the storage account.
questions.explain: BACKUP DATABASE ... TO URL = 'https://...' points the backup at Azure Blob Storage instead of a local disk path. A one-time CREATE CREDENTIAL step, holding a storage account key or SAS token, is what lets SQL Server actually authenticate to that storage account before the backup can run.

questions.prompt: A single compute node hosting a General Purpose–tier Azure SQL Database fails, and a new compute node automatically reattaches to the same remote storage within seconds, with no data loss. Which concept does this scenario actually demonstrate?
options: High availability — surviving a local failure within a region, since the data itself was never touched because it lives on separate remote storage
Disaster recovery — surviving the loss of an entire Azure region
Long-term retention — recovering a backup taken years earlier for a compliance requirement
An Azure SQL failover group's automatic failover policy, since the compute change happened automatically
questions.explain: This is General Purpose's own HA mechanism: compute and storage are separated, so a failed compute node is simply swapped for a new one that reattaches to the same durable storage. HA answers 'what happens when a node fails' within a region — it says nothing about surviving a regional disaster, which is what DR mechanisms like geo-replication or failover groups exist for.

questions.prompt: A business states: "Our order-processing database can't lose more than a few minutes of orders, and we need to be back within 30 minutes if it goes down." Per Lesson 83's process, what should a DBA do with this statement before picking any HA/DR technology?
options: Convert it into explicit numbers — an RPO of about 5 minutes and an RTO of 30 minutes — and only then choose a mechanism actually capable of hitting both
Immediately configure Always On Availability Groups, since it is the most capable HA technology available and will satisfy any stated requirement
Treat the statement as already final, since "a few minutes" and "30 minutes" are precise enough to build a backup schedule around without further translation
Default to nightly full backups, since RPO and RTO are set by whichever backup type the DBA already happens to have configured
questions.explain: RPO and RTO are business decisions stated in plain language first, then written down as explicit numbers in minutes or hours — only after that does a DBA pick a technology capable of hitting those specific numbers. Picking a technology first and hoping it happens to satisfy the business runs the process backwards.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Always On Availability Groups, per Lesson 84.
options: A synchronous replica makes automatic failover possible because the secondary is guaranteed to already be current with the primary
An asynchronous replica adds no latency penalty to the primary's writes, but can lose recently committed transactions if the primary fails before the secondary catches up
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP ... FAILOVER (without FORCE) is the correct command to fail over cleanly to an asynchronous replica
Every database in an Availability Group fails over together, as a single named unit, rather than individually
Synchronous commit guarantees zero added latency on every write, since the secondary never actually needs to be contacted
questions.explain: Synchronous commit guarantees the secondary is current, which is exactly what makes automatic, no-data-loss failover possible — at the cost of waiting on a network round-trip for every write, not zero latency. Asynchronous commit removes that wait but can lose very recent transactions on failover. Plain FAILOVER only works safely against a synchronous replica; failing over to an asynchronous replica requires FORCE_FAILOVER_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS specifically because it can lose data. An AG's defining behavior is that every database in it fails over together as one unit.

questions.prompt: Match each HA/DR mechanism to the characteristic that actually defines it, per Lessons 85-88.
right: Fails over the entire SQL Server instance at once, using shared storage that every cluster node points at
Up to 4 continuously readable secondaries in another region, always asynchronous, promoted manually unless something else is layered on top
Adds a stable listener endpoint on top of geo-replication so the application never has to know which region is currently primary
A periodic backup-copy-restore cycle run by SQL Server Agent jobs, with RPO bounded by the log-backup interval
questions.explain: An FCI fails over the whole instance using shared storage — there's no per-database granularity. Active geo-replication gives up to 4 independently readable, always-asynchronous secondaries, promoted by a manual, explicit action unless a failover group sits on top. A failover group's actual contribution is the stable listener endpoint, not the replication itself. Log shipping is just backup, copy, and restore, repeated on a schedule — its RPO is whatever that schedule is.

questions.prompt: Put these checks of a real HA/DR failover test, per Lesson 89, in the order the lesson lays them out for verifying a failover genuinely worked.
items: Verify the failover itself completes, with the secondary actually becoming primary within the expected RTO
Confirm the application reconnects through the correct endpoint, not a hardcoded old server name somewhere in its configuration
Check that the data loss experienced matches the expected RPO, not more
Test failing back to the original primary afterward, since that is a separate, real operation of its own
questions.explain: Lesson 89 walks through these four checks in this order: does the failover complete within RTO, does the application actually reconnect, does the resulting data loss match the promised RPO, and finally, can you fail back to the original primary. Each one catches a different way a plan that looks correct on paper can still fail silently during a real disaster.

questions.prompt: At Meridian Fleet Logistics (Lesson 91), OrderManagement and DriverHR are joined together by a nightly SQL Server Agent job, while Telemetry is a single fast-growing, append-heavy table with no cross-database dependency. Why did these two groups of databases get two different Azure deployment targets?
options: OrderManagement and DriverHR depend on cross-database queries and an Agent job that Azure SQL Database can't support, so they move to Managed Instance, while Telemetry has neither dependency and fits Azure SQL Database's Hyperscale tier instead
All three databases should have moved to the same Azure SQL Database tier, since giving them different deployment targets creates unnecessary operational inconsistency
Telemetry needed Managed Instance specifically because of its sensitive data, while OrderManagement and DriverHR could use Azure SQL Database since they contain nothing sensitive
The deployment targets were chosen purely by database size, with the two larger databases going to a VM and the smallest one to Azure SQL Database
questions.explain: Azure SQL Database can't run cross-database queries or SQL Server Agent jobs — both of which OrderManagement and DriverHR currently rely on — which is why they move to Managed Instance instead. Telemetry has neither dependency; it's a single, fast-growing, append-heavy table, which is exactly the workload Hyperscale is built for. The two different targets reflect two genuinely different workloads, not an inconsistency.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the security controls chosen for DriverHR in Lesson 91.
options: The shared SQL login is replaced with Microsoft Entra ID authentication, with each team given its own least-privilege database role
TDE alone is treated as sufficient protection for the SSN and license columns, since encrypting data at rest also addresses who can read it live in the table
Always Encrypted is applied to the SSN and license columns so the plaintext stays unreadable even to someone with database access
Support staff who only need to confirm a license number without seeing its full value get Dynamic Data Masking instead of full plaintext access
SQL Auditing is turned on specifically so "nobody's checked access in years" becomes an actual, reviewable log going forward
questions.explain: Entra ID authentication with per-team least-privilege roles replaces the shared login. TDE is explicitly called out as protecting data at rest only, not from a DBA or app running a live query — that's why Always Encrypted, not TDE alone, is applied to the SSN and license columns. Dynamic Data Masking is used for staff who only need a partial confirmation, not the full value. SQL Auditing directly answers Compliance's "nobody's checked in years" concern by making access reviewable going forward.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 93, Meridian's leadership states, "if our primary site goes down, we can lose no more than 15 minutes of data" — a DBA names this directly as an RPO of ________.
questions.explain: "No more than 15 minutes of data" is a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) stated as 15 minutes. Naming the number explicitly, before reaching for an architecture, is the actual skill Lesson 93 is built around — picking a mechanism first and hoping it satisfies the business runs the process backwards.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 95's guidance for answering a scenario-based DBA interview question, what shape should the strongest answer actually follow?
options: Clarify the actual constraint, name the relevant tool or concept, explain the trade-off it involves, then state what you'd verify afterward
Recite the textbook definition of the relevant feature first, then mention a tool only if time allows
Name the most advanced-sounding Azure feature available, since interviewers are primarily testing vocabulary
Ask the interviewer to supply the RPO and RTO numbers directly, since those are rarely stated in a real interview question
questions.explain: Lesson 95 describes this exact four-part shape — clarify the constraint, name the tool, explain the trade-off, state what you'd verify afterward — as what separates a strong, understood answer from a memorized definition, and it's the same shape Chapter 15's capstone project made you practice on one continuous scenario.
